title: From BSE’s banyan tree to blockchain: How Fadnavis wants Mumbai to reinvent finance, again- Moneycontrol.com
text:
My Alerts Go Ad-Free Follow us on: Devendra Fadnavis’s land-tokenisation plan is the latest chapter in Mumbai’s 170-year journey from informal share trading to demat and UPI. But Bengaluru and GIFT City are redrawing India’s financial map.   September 09, 2026 / 13:44 IST             Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis on Wednesday pitched Mumbai as the city where the future of global finance should be designed, as he announced work on what the state says will be India’s first legislative framework for land tokenisation. The proposed  Maharashtra Digitisation and Exchange of Land Tokenisation Act will be backed by a blockchain framework  developed with expertise from SEBI, BSE, NSE, industry and academia, Fadnavis said at Global Fintech Fest 2026. “The future of finance has already started looking beyond New York, London and Singapore and is being built in India,” Fadnavis said. His invitation to innovators was equally direct: “Don’t look at Maharashtra only as your market, but as your laboratory.” The pitch may sound futuristic, but it belongs to an old Mumbai tradition. For nearly two centuries, the city has rebuilt Indian finance after booms, breakdowns and technological shocks. Before Dalal Street had a trading floor, a ticker or even a street address, it had a banyan tree. When a tree became an exchange In the 1850s, brokers gathered beneath a banyan tree near Bombay’s Town Hall to trade shares. Deals depended on proximity, reputation and the spoken word. SEBI’s historical account says their numbers swelled during the American Civil War, when disrupted US cotton supplies sent buyers to Bombay. The cotton windfall produced new banks, finance companies, shipping ventures and land schemes. Maharashtra’s official gazetteer calls the period 'Share Mania', as securities multiplied and speculation outran the real economy. Then the American war ended in 1865. Cotton prices fell, shares collapsed, and fortunes disappeared. Bombay’s first great financial boom had delivered its first modern market crash. The wreckage did not end trading. It created pressure for rules and a permanent institution. Brokers eventually settled in the lane that became Dalal Street. In 1875, they formed the Native Share and Stock Brokers’ Association, now known as BSE. From the colonial port to the regulatory capital Bombay’s port connected merchants, insurers, banks and trading houses to global capital. Its financial pull was such that the Reserve Bank of India, established in 1935 with its central office in Calcutta, moved that office permanently to Bombay in 1937. Mumbai’s next reinvention followed another crisis. The 1992 securities scam exposed weaknesses in settlement systems, bank receipts and the paper-heavy market, accelerating a sweeping overhaul. SEBI received statutory powers in 1992. NSE began operations in 1994, bringing nationwide screen-based trading to a market dominated by the physical ring. NSDL followed in 1996, replacing share certificates vulnerable to delay, theft, forgery and bad delivery with electronic holdings. The market moved from place and paper to networks and verified electronic records. Mumbai remained at the centre, but participation no longer required being in Mumbai. The financial city moves north The city’s financial geography changed too. The old South Mumbai core around Dalal Street and Mint Street gained a northern counterpart in the Bandra-Kurla Complex. BKC was conceived in 1958 to ease pressure on South Mumbai. It eventually drew banks, regulators and exchanges, including SEBI and NSE. Global Fintech Fest is being staged in this newer financial city. The journey runs from a tree, to a street, to a planned business district, and now to networks with no meaningful physical address. The next leap came through payments. NPCI was incorporated in 2008, and UPI launched in Mumbai in 2016 with 21 banks. By 2025-26, UPI accounted for 84 percent of India’s digital payment transactions, government data showed. This is the democratisation Fadnavis referred to. Payments that once needed cash, a cheque, a card terminal or a branch visit were reduced to a phone and an identifier. Can India now do the same for credit, investment and ownership? Can land become a financial rail? Land tokenisation is a far harder test than moving money. Digitisation converts paper records into electronic files. Blockchain can make approved entries difficult to alter undetected. Tokenisation represents a right or economic interest in a digital unit that could be transferred, divided or pledged. Cleaner records and programmable transactions could shorten verification, expose encumbrances, widen access to collateral and put capital locked in property to productive use, while leaving an audit trail. But blockchain cannot decide who owns a disputed plot. Indian land records generally provide presumptive rather than state-guaranteed title, PRS Legislative Research notes. Deeds, revenue records, maps, inheritance claims, mortgages, tenancy rights and possession may tell different stories. Putting an unverified claim on an immutable ledger can create a perfect record of an imperfect claim. The law’s details will matter more than the word blockchain. Will a token represent legal title, a beneficial interest or merely a recorded transaction? Who can freeze it during litigation? How will court orders, stamp duty, mutation and KYC checks be integrated? How will small landholders be protected? SEBI, BSE and NSE can bring expertise in market design, disclosure, surveillance and settlement. Yet land is governed by state laws and local records. Technology can reinforce a trusted legal system; it cannot substitute for one. Mumbai must win its title again Fadnavis’s global-finance pitch also arrives amid sharper domestic competition. Bengaluru remains India’s dominant technology and startup centre. Tracxn data for the first half of 2026 showed it drew about 70 per cent of the country’s fintech funding, well ahead of Mumbai. GIFT City in Gujarat, meanwhile, offers a purpose-built international financial services centre with its own regulatory architecture. Mumbai’s history is an advantage, not a guarantee. Its leadership has endured because the city repeatedly replaced failing systems with stronger institutions. The banyan-tree gathering became an exchange. Paper certificates became demat accounts. Bank transfers became instant mobile payments. The same standard will judge the proposed land-tokenisation framework: not whether it sounds new, but whether it makes ownership safer, access wider and transactions more trustworthy. Fadnavis told the audience that trust is the technology on which every other technology rests. Mumbai’s financial history makes the point better than any slogan. The city’s next reinvention will not be secured by blockchain alone. It will depend on whether law, records and accountability can move with it. The city’s financial geography changed too. The old South Mumbai core around Dalal Street and Mint Street gained a northern counterpart in the Bandra-Kurla Complex.

BKC was conceived in 1958 to ease pressure on South Mumbai. It eventually drew banks, regulators and exchanges, including SEBI and NSE. Global Fintech Fest is being staged in this newer financial city.
